title: My Summer With the Humanities and What It Taught Me About Ausubel's Meaningful Learning
author: Lstam
summary: A third-grade teacher recounts taking Ted Gioia's 12-week humanities course over the summer — 250 pages a week of ancient-world texts alongside related music and art — not to build grade-specific content knowledge but to broaden her general humanities background, and discovers an unexpected pedagogical lesson in the process. The course turned out to function as an in-depth review that connected previously isolated pieces of knowledge from her second- and third-grade teaching (Ancient Greece, China, India, Rome) into a single coherent schema, deepening her own understanding of how ancient civilizations influenced each other and modern events. She explicitly maps this personal experience onto David Ausubel's theory of meaningful learning, recognizing that her own students likely hold the same kind of isolated, disconnected civilization knowledge from earlier grades that she held before the course connected hers. This realization becomes a concrete instructional commitment: she will intentionally review prior-grade content, explicitly connect new material to what students already learned, and design lessons that push students toward the 'generalization and adaptation' phases of the instructional hierarchy rather than leaving civilization units as isolated, disconnected topics.
points: The article's core insight is experiential, not just theoretical: the teacher only recognized the risk of isolated, unconnected knowledge in her students after experiencing the opposite — connected, schema-building knowledge — in her own humanities course.

She identifies a specific, common curriculum design flaw: teaching Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, India, and Greece as separate grade-level units without explicit connections between them increases the likelihood students will forget what they learned, since isolated facts lack the retrieval cues that a connected schema provides.

Her three concrete instructional commitments — intentionally reviewing earlier-grade content, explicitly connecting new content to it, and designing toward the 'generalization and adaptation' phases of the instructional hierarchy — translate an abstract theory (Ausubel's meaningful learning) into a specific lesson-planning checklist.

The piece models a form of teacher professional development that doesn't map directly onto classroom content but still yields classroom-relevant insight, reinforcing the value of teachers building broad content knowledge rather than only grade-specific knowledge.
quotes: Traditionally, I would build my content knowledge specific to the content I teach for my grade level. For example, when I taught second grade, I focused on building my knowledge of Ancient Greece, Ancient China, Ancient India.

It took that knowledge I had acquired over several years, which had been somewhat isolated bits of knowledge, and connected it all into one schema. It made that knowledge stronger and deeper, and gave me a better picture of the ancient world as a whole.

Through my own summer learning experience, I realized that I need to intentionally design my lessons to build and strengthen connections between knowledge my students learned in earlier grades and what they will learn this year.
Their knowledge of each civilization is isolated, and they are unaware of the connections across the content. This also increases the likelihood they will forget what they have learned.

Intentionally review content they have learned in earlier grades. Explicitly connect third grade content to content learned in earlier grades. Design learning experiences that advance students towards the generalization and adaptation phases of the instructional hierarchy so they can build connections across content.
